FAMILY ALLOWANCE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Pat Morgan

PROPOSED PETITIONER — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF A FAMILY ALLOWANCE PETITION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, am the person seeking a family allowance from the estate of Pat Morgan, who died on June 1, 2026. My relationship to Pat Morgan is: Surviving spouse. This declaration relates to a proceeding in the estate of Pat Morgan, to be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of Alameda County, under Probate Code §§ 6540-6545. The monthly family allowance amount I am requesting is: $3,000 per month. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for family allowance. It is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not grant, modify, or set the amount of any family allowance for Jordan Alex Lee or anyone else — only a court order, issued after the statutory petition and (where required) notice process described in this document, can do that.

WHO MAY RECEIVE A FAMILY ALLOWANCE, AND THE STANDARD THE COURT APPLIES
Probate Code § 6540(a) entitles three categories of people to a reasonable family allowance out of Pat Morgan's estate — an amount necessary for their maintenance according to their circumstances during administration of the estate: the surviving spouse of Pat Morgan; Pat Morgan's minor children; and Pat Morgan's adult children who are physically or mentally incapacitated from earning a living and were actually dependent in whole or in part on Pat Morgan for support. § 6540(b) separately allows the court, in its discretion, to give a reasonable family allowance to two further categories on the same maintenance-according-to-circumstances standard: other adult children of Pat Morgan who were actually dependent in whole or in part on Pat Morgan for support, and a parent of Pat Morgan who was actually dependent in whole or in part on Pat Morgan for support. § 6540(c) limits both categories: if a person otherwise eligible for a family allowance has reasonable maintenance from other sources and there are one or more other persons entitled to a family allowance, the allowance is granted only to those who do not have reasonable maintenance from other sources.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The following are entitled to such reasonable family allowance out of the estate as is necessary for their maintenance according to their circumstances during administration of the estate: (1) The surviving spouse of the decedent. (2) Minor children of the decedent. (3) Adult children of the decedent who are physically or mentally incapacitated from earning a living and were actually dependent in whole or in part upon the decedent for support."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6540(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6540(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6540.)
  "The following may be given such reasonable family allowance out of the estate as the court in its discretion determines is necessary for their maintenance according to their circumstances during administration of the estate: (1) Other adult children of the decedent who were actually dependent in whole or in part upon the decedent for support. (2) A parent of the decedent who was actually dependent in whole or in part upon the decedent for support."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6540(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6540(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6540.)
  "If a person otherwise eligible for family allowance has a reasonable maintenance from other sources and there are one or more other persons entitled to a family allowance, the family allowance shall be granted only to those who do not have a reasonable maintenance from other sources."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6540(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6540(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6540.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about whether any specific person qualifies under it. This clause quotes three parts of a single statutory section (§ 6540(a), (b), and (c)); no independent second section was found addressing eligibility itself, so this clause relies on one section only. § 6540 states the maintenance-according-to-circumstances standard as the basis for both the entitled and discretionary categories, but this statute does not itself list the specific factors a court weighs in fixing a dollar amount (for example, the estate's size or the claimant's other income) beyond that general standard; this clause does not attempt to supply factors the statute's text does not state. This document is informational: it does not itself grant a family allowance, determine any specific person's eligibility, or set any dollar amount — only a court order can do that.

WHO MAY PETITION, AND THE EX PARTE OPTION BEFORE THE INVENTORY IS FILED
Probate Code § 6541(a) lets the court grant or modify a family allowance for Pat Morgan's estate on petition of any interested person — not only the person who would receive the allowance. § 6541(b) then ties the procedure to timing relative to the inventory: before the inventory is filed, an order for the § 6540(a)-entitled allowance may be made or modified either ex parte or after notice of the hearing has been given as provided in Probate Code § 1220; after the inventory is filed, such an order may be made or modified only after that § 1220 notice has been given. § 6541(c) requires that a § 6540(b)-discretionary allowance be ordered only after § 1220 notice has been given to each person listed in § 1220, each known heir whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition, and each known devisee whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The court may grant or modify a family allowance on petition of any interested person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6541(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6541(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6541.)
  "With respect to an order for the family allowance provided for in subdivision (a) of Section 6540: (1) Before the inventory is filed, the order may be made or modified either (A) ex parte or (B) after notice of the hearing on the petition has been given as provided in Section 1220. (2) After the inventory is filed, the order may be made or modified only after notice of the hearing on the petition has been given as provided in Section 1220."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6541(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6541(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6541.)
  "An order for the family allowance provided in subdivision (b) of Section 6540 may be made only after notice of the hearing on the petition has been given as provided in Section 1220 to all of the following persons: (1) Each person listed in Section 1220. (2) Each known heir whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition. (3) Each known devisee whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6541(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6541(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6541.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This clause quotes three subdivisions of a single statutory section (§ 6541(a), (b), and (c)); no independent second section was found addressing the petition-and-notice procedure itself. § 6541(b)(1)(A)'s ex parte option — available only before the inventory is filed, and only for the § 6540(a) categories — is the statute's mechanism for obtaining an allowance before a noticed hearing can be held; this clause does not independently verify the content of the § 1220 notice requirements themselves, referencing § 1220 only as the notice provision § 6541 points to. This document is informational: it does not itself petition for, grant, or modify any family allowance, or give any specific notice — only an actual petition, followed by a court order (and, where required, notice under § 1220), can do that.

WHEN A FAMILY ALLOWANCE BEGINS, AND HOW FAR BACK IT MAY REACH
Probate Code § 6542 lets a family allowance for Pat Morgan's estate commence on the date of the court's order, or on such other date as the court's order provides, whether that date is before or after the date of the order, as the court in its discretion determines. The one fixed limit is that the allowance may not be made retroactive to a date earlier than Pat Morgan's date of death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A family allowance commences on the date of the court’s order or such other time as may be provided in the court’s order, whether before or after the date of the order, as the court in its discretion determines, but the allowance may not be made retroactive to a date earlier than the date of the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6542 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6542 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6542.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about what commencement date any specific court would set. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 6542); no independent second section was found addressing the commencement date itself. Read together with the companion clause on § 6541, the earliest a family allowance can practically start flowing is set by when a petition (potentially ex parte, before the inventory is filed) is granted, while the earliest date the order itself may reach back to is the decedent's date of death; this clause does not resolve, for any specific estate, how a court would exercise its discretion between those two points. This document is informational: it does not itself set any commencement date or grant any family allowance — only a court order does that.

HOW LONG A FAMILY ALLOWANCE CONTINUES
Probate Code § 6543(a) fixes an outer limit on a family allowance for Pat Morgan's estate: it must terminate no later than the entry of the order for final distribution of the estate, or, if the estate is insolvent, no later than one year after the granting of letters. Within that limit, § 6543(b) provides that the allowance continues until modified or terminated by the court, or until such time as the court's order itself provides.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A family allowance shall terminate no later than the entry of the order for final distribution of the estate or, if the estate is insolvent, no later than one year after the granting of letters."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6543(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6543(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6543.)
  "Subject to subdivision (a), a family allowance shall continue until modified or terminated by the court or until such time as the court may provide in its order."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6543(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6543(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6543.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about how long any specific allowance would run. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single statutory section (§ 6543(a) and (b)); no independent second section was found addressing duration itself. This clause does not independently verify the statutory definition of estate insolvency used in § 6543(a), or the point at which letters are considered granted for purposes of that one-year outer limit. This document is informational: it does not itself continue, modify, or terminate any family allowance — only a court order (or the passage of the statutory outer limit) does that.

THE ESTATE, NOT THE PETITIONER PERSONALLY, BEARS THE COSTS OF A FAMILY ALLOWANCE PROCEEDING
Probate Code § 6544 provides that the costs of proceedings under the family allowance chapter — the chapter under which a petition for Pat Morgan's estate would be brought — are paid by the estate as expenses of administration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The costs of proceedings under this chapter shall be paid by the estate as expenses of administration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6544 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6544 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6544.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about what specific costs any specific petition would generate. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 6544); no independent second section was found addressing costs of the proceeding itself. This clause does not address attorney's fees separately from costs, and does not independently verify how 'expenses of administration' is defined elsewhere in the Probate Code for purposes of this section. This document is informational: it does not itself allocate any specific cost to any specific estate — only a court order does that.

WHERE A FAMILY ALLOWANCE RANKS AMONG THE ESTATE'S OTHER DEBTS
Probate Code § 11420(a) sets a fixed order of priority in which Pat Morgan's estate's debts are paid, apart from debts owed to the United States or California that have their own statutory preference: (1) expenses of administration; (2) obligations secured by a mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien, so far as payable from the proceeds of the property securing them; (3) funeral expenses; (4) expenses of last illness; (5) family allowance; (6) wage claims; and (7) general debts, including unsecured judgments and all other debts not included in a prior class. A family allowance therefore ranks below expenses of administration, secured obligations, funeral expenses, and expenses of last illness, but ahead of wage claims and general debts. § 11420(b) provides that debts within the same class are paid without preference over one another, that no debt of any class may be paid until all debts of prior classes are paid in full, and that if estate property is insufficient to pay a class in full, each debt in that class is paid a proportionate share.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Debts shall be paid in the following order of priority among classes of debts, except that debts owed to the United States or to this state that have preference under the laws of the United States or of this state shall be given the preference required by such laws: (1) Expenses of administration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 11420(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 11420(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=11420.)
  "(3) Funeral expenses. (4) Expenses of last illness. (5) Family allowance. (6) Wage claims. (7) General debts, including judgments not secured by a lien and all other debts not included in a prior class."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 11420(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 11420(a)(3)-(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=11420.)
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, the debts of each class are without preference or priority one over another. No debt of any class may be paid until all those of prior classes are paid in full. If property in the estate is insufficient to pay all debts of any class in full, each debt in that class shall be paid a proportionate share."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 11420(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 11420(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=11420.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's debt-payment priority scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about whether any specific estate's assets are sufficient to reach the family-allowance class. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single statutory section (§ 11420(a) and (b)); no independent second section was found addressing this priority order itself. This clause condenses § 11420(a)'s seven-class list and omits the full text of class (2) (the treatment of secured obligations and any shortfall reclassified as a general debt) beyond the summary given here; the full text is available at the cited source. This document is informational: it does not itself pay any debt, allowance, or class of claims, or determine solvency for any specific estate — only the personal representative's administration of the estate, under court supervision where required, does that.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — FAMILY ALLOWANCE INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 3, 2026 at Oakland, California.
